answer: A place where I learned something genuinely new was a small pottery studio in Dhaka, where I took a one-day weekend workshop while I was staying with my elder sister last year. I had always been curious about working with clay, partly because Bengal has such a long tradition of terracotta and clay pots, so when my sister showed me an advert online, I signed up [[on a whim]]. What I learned was the basics of shaping clay on a potter's wheel, from centring the lump of clay to slowly pulling up the walls of a bowl. From the moment I sat at the wheel, I realised how much more [[demanding]] the craft is than it looks. My first few attempts collapsed hopelessly, which was [[humbling]] but oddly enjoyable. The instructor was wonderfully patient, guiding us step by step, sometimes placing her hands over ours so we could feel the right pressure, until I finally shaped something recognisable. There were only six of us, so we got plenty of individual attention and learned a lot from each other's mistakes as well. What I found most valuable was learning to be patient with myself; the process required real [[perseverance]]. There was something deeply satisfying about creating something with my own hands, away from screens. By the end of the day I had made a slightly wobbly bowl that I was absurdly proud of, and it now sits on my desk at home. Honestly, the experience was surprisingly [[therapeutic]], and it reminded me how rewarding it is to step outside your [[comfort zone]].

followUps.q: Have you done pottery since then?
followUps.answer: Not yet, unfortunately, because there is no studio near Sirajganj. But I have been looking for another workshop in Dhaka, and I would love to try again and hopefully make something less wobbly.

followUps.q: Do you think adults should keep learning new skills?
followUps.answer: Absolutely. Learning something new keeps your mind active and stops life from becoming routine. It does not have to be useful for work; even a hobby like pottery can teach you patience and confidence.
